quicknotes_mcp tools/list response (tool names and descriptions)
Content returned by quicknotes_mcp tool calls

slack-mcp (local MCP server wrapping the Slack API)

controls.name: Filesystem MCP server scoped to a single directory (C:/Users/dev)
controls.decay_rationale: The directory scope is enforced by the filesystem server itself regardless of model capability, but it does not exclude sensitive subpaths such as .aws or .ssh that live inside the same home directory, so it does not constrain the sink of the credential-exfiltration path.

controls.name: Desktop client approval prompt on first call per tool, remembered thereafter
controls.decay_rationale: The first-call dialog does not itself depend on model capability, but because the decision is remembered as 'always allow,' every subsequent call to the same tool, including the poisoned add_note call shown here, proceeds with no review at all. It is not a per-call gate and earns no residual credit.

controls.name: Pin and hash MCP tool/server definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Version pinning blocks silent redefinition regardless of model capability; it fails only if its owner disables it (control_removal) or a new, unpinned-by-default server is added.

controls.name: Injection classifier on third-party tool descriptions and tool output
controls.decay_rationale: A separate classifier can catch a simple imperative payload like the <IMPORTANT> block shown here, but multi-turn or obfuscated payloads get past it, and it does not scale with a more capable attacker-directed model.

controls.name: Exclude credential and secret paths from filesystem server scope
controls.decay_rationale: A directory scope that structurally excludes ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, and similar paths removes the sensitive file from the reachable set regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for quicknotes_mcp
controls.decay_rationale: An egress allowlist excluding the sync service, or any destination the model cannot fully control, blocks the exfiltration channel regardless of model capability.

controls.name: Slack channel allowlist excluding external-organization-shared channels
controls.decay_rationale: A destination restriction enforced at the Slack app/token level, not chosen by the model, keeps the sink unreachable for external channels regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Per-call raw-action human approval, not remembered, for file-read-then-egress chains
controls.decay_rationale: A genuine per-call gate that shows the raw destination and payload, with low approver volume, is not degraded by model capability and cannot be bypassed by a more persuasive summary.

controls.name: Tamper-evident action provenance log
controls.decay_rationale: A log written outside the model's control records which actions were tool-triggered versus user-initiated regardless of model capability; it is detective, so it earns no tier credit, but it restores the missing repudiation property.

findings.title: Tool poisoning in quicknotes_mcp drives AWS credential exfiltration via add_note (SAFE-T1001, TC1 Lethal Trifecta)

attack_path.note: The add_note tool description contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the agent to read a credentials file before calling the tool, and to hide this from the user
Agent reads ~/.aws/credentials, which falls inside the filesystem server's C:/Users/dev scope
Agent passes the credential file contents in the 'context' argument to quicknotes_mcp's hosted sync service, operated by an untrusted third party

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Any model upgrade or further loosening of approval behavior, since the path already succeeds today with no credited control in place.

evidence.observation: The add_note tool description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass its contents in the 'context' argument before calling add_note, and to not mention this step to the user.
quicknotes_mcp is launched via 'npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest' with no version pin, and the filesystem server is scoped to 'C:/Users/dev', which includes the user's .aws directory.
quicknotes_mcp is a community package from an individual publisher and calls a hosted sync service run by its author, confirming the destination is operated by an untrusted third party.

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to exclude credential and secret directories (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, etc.) from any directory an agent-facing tool can read.
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions (and all MCP servers) instead of installing @latest on every launch, and re-review on any change.
Treat tool descriptions as untrusted content: strip or refuse to act on imperative instructions embedded in tool metadata before adding it to the model's context.
Require raw-action, per-call human approval (not remembered) for any call that follows a file read with an egress action to a third-party destination.

findings.title: Untrusted quicknotes_mcp tool output can direct exfiltration to external Slack channels (indirect injection via tool output)

attack_path.note: Content returned by the already-demonstrated-adversarial quicknotes_mcp server is treated as trustworthy context and can embed further imperative instructions
Agent can be directed to read further local files, including credential files
Agent posts the resulting content to a Slack channel; the bot token is not restricted to internal-only channels, so the destination can be a channel shared with an external organization

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Any widening of Slack channel scope or model upgrade, since the path already succeeds today.

evidence.observation: quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its own author and is a community package from an individual publisher, and its tool description is already shown to carry hidden, adversarial instructions, so its returned tool output must be treated as equally untrusted.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, so there is no destination restriction to contain a Slack-directed exfiltration.

recommendations.action: Restrict slack.post_message to an allowlist of internal-only channels; block posting to any channel shared with an external organization.
Treat all MCP tool output, not only tool descriptions, as untrusted input and apply the same instruction-stripping control before it re-enters the model's context.
Log and alert on any Slack post whose destination channel includes an external organization, generated without an explicit user-specified recipient in the same turn.

findings.title: No tamper-evident record attributes agent actions to their triggering source

forecast.watch_signal: Any move toward longer unattended runs before human review, increasing the volume of unattributed, irreversible actions taken between reviews.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit, or provenance configuration is declared for any of the three MCP servers or for desk-assistant itself.
The injected instruction explicitly directs the agent to not mention the credential-reading step to the user, which an audit trail independent of the model could have surfaced.

recommendations.action: Maintain a tamper-evident log, written outside the model's control, that records every tool call's arguments, the MCP server/tool version that produced any triggering instruction, and whether the action was user-initiated or tool-triggered.

findings.title: No version pinning on any MCP server allows silent redefinition of tool behavior at next launch (MCP Rug Pull)

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

forecast.watch_signal: Any new version of filesystem, slack, or quicknotes_mcp being installed automatically via @latest with no diff review.

evidence.observation: All three MCP servers are launched with 'npx -y <package>@latest', meaning the exact code and tool definitions used can change between runs without any version pin or review.

recommendations.action: Pin all three MCP servers to specific, reviewed versions or content hashes, and require manual re-approval on any version or tool-schema change.

stride_coverage.rationale: desk-assistant is a local desktop client process invoked directly by its authenticated user; no external peer or protocol in this design allows another entity to impersonate the agent itself.
No capability or input in this design allows modification of desk-assistant's own system prompt, configuration, or installed tool set; self-modification is not asserted.
Runtime notes do not state step limits, timeouts, or spend caps for desk-assistant; there is insufficient evidence to assess runaway-loop or resource-exhaustion risk.
Artifacts do not describe authentication or peer identity verification for the filesystem MCP server; insufficient evidence to assess spoofing risk.
No logging or attribution mechanism for filesystem server actions is described in the provided artifacts.
The filesystem server only performs synchronous local file reads scoped to a directory; the design gives no basis for a resource-exhaustion pathway distinct from desk-assistant's own entry.
Artifacts do not describe authentication or identity verification for the slack-mcp server itself, beyond the bot token used against the Slack API.
No rate limit or posting cap on slack.post_message is described; insufficient evidence to assess a flooding or denial-of-service pathway.

This flow carries tool metadata from quicknotes_mcp into the agent's context; it does not itself carry confidential data outward, so outbound disclosure is scored on the downstream egress flows instead.
A one-time tools/list response of bounded size does not present a volumetric denial-of-service vector distinct from the goal-hijack risk already captured in F1.
This inbound flow carries notes content from quicknotes_mcp into the agent's context; it does not itself move the user's data outward, so outbound disclosure is scored on the egress flows instead.
Artifacts do not describe response size limits or timeouts on quicknotes_mcp output; insufficient evidence to assess a flooding vector.
The flow carries arguments from desk-assistant to quicknotes_mcp.add_note over local stdio; no in-transit tampering vector distinct from the payload-content risk already captured in F1 is described.
No rate limit on add_note calls is described; insufficient evidence to assess a volumetric abuse vector.
The flow carries arguments from desk-assistant to slack.post_message over the Slack API; no in-transit tampering vector distinct from the payload-content risk already captured in F2 is described.
No posting rate limit is described for slack.post_message; insufficient evidence to assess spam or flooding risk.

rating.rationale: desk-assistant's filesystem, quicknotes, and Slack capabilities form a lethal-trifecta chain (F1) confirmed directly by a poisoned tool description instructing the agent to read AWS credentials and exfiltrate them through quicknotes_mcp's third-party sync service; the same adversarial-server assumption extends to tool output and a second egress channel through an unrestricted Slack bot (F2). No credited control currently blocks either path: the only approval step is a one-time, rememberable prompt that earns no credit under the rubric, and the filesystem server's directory scope does not exclude the credentials file. Two further property findings record a missing action-provenance log (F3) and the lack of version pinning across all three MCP servers (F4), both rated high. Residual equals inherent because no structural control severs the path, narrows and constrains the sink, or gates it with a real per-call approval; forecast equals residual because the path already succeeds under present-day model capability, so no trigger can raise it further.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of desk-assistant.
No system prompt for desk-assistant was provided, so goal framing, explicit safety instructions, and any agent-level guardrails are not assessed.
Only one example of a poisoned tool description was provided; finding F2 extrapolates the same adversarial-server assumption to tool output and is rated with medium rather than high confidence.

autonomy.level is inferred as A3 because the described 'remembered approval' does not function as a per-step or per-sensitive-action gate; if the client in fact re-prompts under conditions not described here, this could change.
